tool.name: Git
tool.tagline: Distributed version control for tracking and sharing code changes
tool.description: Git records the history of a project as a series of snapshots and lets many people work on it in parallel through branches, merges and remotes. It is the version control system behind GitHub, GitLab and nearly every software team, so fluency in it is a baseline skill for any developer.

glossary.def: One saved version of a project in Git: a snapshot of all its files plus a short message saying what changed, who made it and when.
The unique code Git gives each commit, like 3f9a2c1. It is calculated from the commit's contents, so a changed commit gets a new ID.
The ordinary files in your project folder that you see and edit, as opposed to the history Git keeps in the hidden .git folder.
Git's draft of your next commit. You copy changes into it with git add, and git commit saves exactly what is in it. Git's commands also call it the index.
Git's name for the commit you currently have in front of you. Usually it points at your current branch, which points at that branch's latest commit.
A separate, named line of work in a Git repository. Technically just a movable label pointing at a commit; it moves forward each time you commit on it.
A website, such as GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, that stores copies of Git repositories online so people can share them, and adds team features like review pages.
A complete copy of a Git repository, history included, usually downloaded from a server with git clone.
A short name (such as origin) that your repository uses for another copy of it, usually on a server, saved together with that copy's address.
Your repository's note of where a branch on a remote was the last time you talked to it, such as origin/main. It updates only when you fetch, pull or push.
The branch on a remote that your local branch is paired with, so git push and git pull know where to send and fetch, and git status can say ahead or behind.
Your own copy of someone else's repository on a hosting site, where you can push changes and then propose them back to the original.
Updating a branch by simply moving it ahead to newer commits built on top of it, so nothing has to be combined and no extra commit is made.
Combining the work of two branches into one. When both have new commits, Git records the result as a merge commit that has both as parents.
A commit with two (or more) previous commits instead of one, recording that two lines of work were joined.
What happens when two changes being combined edited the same lines differently: Git stops, marks the spot in the file and asks you to decide.
The most recent commit two branches have in common: the point where they split. Git compares both sides against it when merging.
Moving your commits so they start from a newer point: Git lifts them off and replays them one by one on top, creating new commits with new IDs.
Combining several commits into a single commit.
A place where git stash puts unfinished changes aside so you get clean files, ready to bring the changes back later.
A permanent name, such as v1.2.0, attached to one specific commit, usually to mark a release. Unlike a branch, it never moves.
The state where HEAD points straight at a commit instead of at a branch. New commits made there belong to no branch unless you create one.
Git's private, local diary of every place HEAD and each branch have pointed to, used to find and recover commits that seem lost.
Copying the change made by one existing commit onto your current branch as a new commit.
Copying a fix from the newest version of a project to an older version that people still use.
Git's tool for finding the commit that introduced a problem by repeatedly testing the commit halfway through the suspect range.
An extra working folder attached to the same repository, so you can have two branches checked out at once in different folders.
A Git repository placed inside another one, where the outer repository records exactly which commit of the inner one to use.
A small program Git runs automatically at a certain moment, such as just before a commit, to check or change something.
Git's general word for a name that points at a commit (or another stored object): branches, tags, remote-tracking branches and HEAD are all refs.
A ref that holds the name of another ref instead of an ID. HEAD is usually one: it says 'refs/heads/main' rather than a commit ID.
One item in Git's internal storage (a file's content, a folder listing, a commit or a tag), saved under an ID calculated from its content.
The Git object holding the raw content of one file, with no name attached. Identical contents anywhere in history share one blob.
The Git object for one folder: a list of names, each pointing at a blob (a file) or another tree object (a subfolder).
One compressed file in which Git bundles many stored objects, saving space by storing similar versions as differences from each other.
In Git's storage, a version of a file kept only as its differences from a similar version, to save space.
Git's low-level commands (like git cat-file) meant for scripts and for looking at internals, as opposed to everyday commands like git commit.
A team workflow where everyone joins their work into the main branch at least daily, using only very short-lived branches.
A branch made for one released version (like release/2.4) so it can get fixes while new work continues on main.
A clone that downloads all commits but fetches the contents of files only when you actually need them.
A clone that downloads only the most recent commits, cutting off older history to save time.
Having only some folders of a big repository present as files on disk, while the history still covers everything.
Git Large File Storage: an add-on that keeps big files such as videos on a separate server and puts only small placeholder files in the repository.

concepts.name: What version control is
concepts.summary: Version control keeps every saved version of a project's files, so you can compare, undo and share work safely.
concepts.why: Almost every software team uses it; without it, working together and recovering from mistakes is guesswork.
concepts.body:
Think about how people often save a document they keep working on: `report.docx`, then `report-v2.docx`, then `report-final.docx`, then `report-final-REALLY.docx`. Soon nobody knows which file is the right one or what changed between them.

**Version control** fixes this properly. A version control system keeps one set of files plus a complete history: every saved version, who made it, when, and a note saying why. Git is by far the most widely used one. It is mostly used for the files of software projects, but it works for any text files.

Each saved version is called a **commit**. A commit is a **snapshot**: a picture of what every file in the project looked like at that moment, plus a short message describing the change. Files that didn't change aren't copied again, so keeping thousands of snapshots stays cheap.

The project folder together with its whole history is called a **repository** (often shortened to *repo*). Git keeps that history inside the project folder itself, on your own computer.

Git is built for teams, too. Everyone has their own complete copy of the repository, history included, which is why Git is called *distributed*. You can save new commits with no internet connection and swap them with others later. Teams usually keep one shared copy on a **server**: a computer that is always switched on and reachable over the internet, so everyone has one agreed place to exchange work.

What you get from it day to day:

- A safety net: you can go back to any commit, so trying things out is never risky.
- Teamwork: several people change the same project at the same time, and Git combines their work.
- Answers: for any line you can find the commit that changed it and read why.
- **Branches**: separate lines of work, like a draft copy of the project where you try an idea and fold it back in once it works.

Git itself is a free program that runs on your computer. Websites such as GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket, called **Git hosting services**, store copies of repositories online and add extras like discussion pages. They're handy, but Git works perfectly well without them.
takeaways: Git saves snapshots of your whole project, called commits, linked into a history
Everyone has a full copy of the repository, so most work happens without a connection
Git is the program; GitHub and GitLab are websites that store repositories online
pitfalls: Thinking Git and GitHub are the same thing — Git runs on your own computer without any account or website.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Git is 'distributed'?
options: Your files are split across several servers
Everyone's copy contains the complete history
Each person may only edit their own files
Every commit is sent to a server immediately
quiz.explain: Each person's copy is a full repository, so history and new commits work without any connection.

quiz.q: What is a commit?
options: A snapshot of the whole project plus a message
A list of typing edits to one file
A zip file uploaded to a website
A copy of only the files you opened today
quiz.explain: A commit records what every file looked like at that moment; unchanged files are shared, not copied again.

concepts.name: Install and configure Git
concepts.summary: Install Git, open a terminal, and tell Git your name and email with git config.
concepts.why: Every commit is stamped with your name and email, and a few settings made now save confusion later.
concepts.body:
You use Git mostly by typing short instructions, called commands, into a **terminal**: a window where you type a line of text, press Enter, and the computer answers in text instead of you clicking buttons. On a Mac it's the Terminal app; on Windows, Git comes with one called *Git Bash*; on Linux, look for Terminal among your apps.

Install Git from git-scm.com, which has a normal installer for Windows and Mac. Then check it worked: type `git --version` and press Enter, and Git prints its version number.

Every Git command starts with `git`, then a word naming the action, like `config` or `commit`, and sometimes options that start with dashes, like `--global`. Before your first commit, tell Git who you are. Your name and email are written into every commit you make, so use the email you want your work linked to, such as the one on your GitHub account:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
```

`git config` saves settings at three levels, and the more specific one wins:

- `--system`: every user account on this computer.
- `--global`: just you, saved in a settings file in your **home folder**, your personal top-level folder (`~/.gitconfig`).
- `--local`: one repository only, saved in `.git/config`. This is the default when you run `git config` inside a project.

So you can use a work email inside work projects only. `git config --list --show-origin` shows every setting and the file it came from.

A few settings worth making on day one:

- `init.defaultBranch main`: new projects start with a branch called `main`, today's usual name.
- `core.editor`: the **text editor** (a program for editing text without formatting, like Notepad) that Git opens when you need to write a longer note, such as a commit message. For example `"code --wait"` for Visual Studio Code, or `nano`, a simple editor inside the terminal.
- `pull.rebase false`: tells Git how to combine your work with teammates' work when you download theirs. You'll learn what it means later; setting it now stops Git asking.

On Windows, `core.autocrlf true` smooths over a small difference: Windows ends each line of text with two invisible characters, Mac and Linux with one.
concepts.code:
git --version                         # git version 2.51.0
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global pull.rebase false

git config user.email                 # show one setting
git config --list --show-origin       # every setting and the file it came from
takeaways: Git is used by typing commands in a terminal
Set user.name and user.email before your first commit
Setting levels: system < global (your home folder) < local (one repository)
git config --list --show-origin shows where each setting comes from
pitfalls: Committing with the wrong email — the commits won't be linked to your account, and fixing old commits later is awkward.

quiz.q: You set user.email with --global, then a different user.email with --local inside project A. Which email do commits in project A use?
quiz.explain: The more specific level wins: local beats global, which beats system.

concepts.name: Create or clone a repository
concepts.summary: Start tracking a project with git init, or download a full copy of an existing repository with git clone.
concepts.why: Every Git workflow starts with a repository; these two commands are how you get one.
concepts.body:
A repository is a normal folder (Git's messages also call folders **directories**) with one extra thing inside: a hidden folder named `.git`. It's hidden because its name starts with a dot, so your computer's file windows don't show it unless you ask. That `.git` folder *is* the repository: it holds every commit and every setting. The ordinary files around it are just the version of the project you're looking at right now.

There are two ways to get one.

**`git init`** turns the folder you are in into a new, empty repository. Git isn't keeping history for any file yet; you choose which files to add. Use it for a brand-new project, or to start keeping history for a folder you already have.

**`git clone <url>`** downloads a complete copy of a repository that lives somewhere else, usually on a server such as GitHub. You give it the repository's **URL**, its web address. Git copies the full history into a new folder, shows you the latest version of the files, and remembers where the copy came from under the short name `origin`. Such a copy is called a **clone**.

Addresses come in two forms. One starts with `https://` and works like signing in to a website: for a private repository, the hosting site asks for a password or a password-like code it gives you. The other starts with `git@` and uses **SSH**: your computer keeps a secret key file that proves who you are, so you don't type anything. Both work; the `https://` form is easier to start with.

You can choose the new folder's name by adding it at the end: `git clone <url> my-app`.

Because all of the history lives in `.git`, deleting that folder deletes the whole history and leaves plain files behind. Renaming the project folder, or putting it somewhere else, is fine; Git doesn't mind where it lives.

Don't create a repository inside another one by accident, for example by running `git init` in your home folder. If you're unsure which repository you're in, `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` prints its folder.
concepts.code:
# Brand-new project
mkdir notes && cd notes       # make a folder called notes and go into it
git init                      # Initialized empty Git repository in .../notes/.git/
ls -a                         # list everything, hidden files too: .  ..  .git

# Copy an existing project with its full history
git clone https://github.com/git/git.git
git clone git@github.com:me/app.git my-app   # SSH address, into folder my-app
cd my-app
git remote -v                 # origin  git@github.com:me/app.git (fetch/push)
takeaways: The hidden .git folder is the repository; the files around it are what you work on
git init starts empty; git clone downloads the full history and remembers it as origin
Web-style addresses use a sign-in; git@ addresses use an SSH key
pitfalls: Running git init in your home folder, which makes every file you own look like part of one project.

quiz.q: What does git clone give you besides the files?
options: Nothing else; history stays on the server
The full history and a remote named origin
quiz.explain: A clone is a copy of the whole repository, and Git records where it came from under the name origin.

concepts.name: Working tree, staging area and history
concepts.summary: Git keeps your changes in three places: the files you edit, a staging area for the next commit, and the saved history.
concepts.why: Almost every Git command is about shifting changes between these areas, so this model makes the rest click.
concepts.body:
Git keeps your project in three places at once. Picture packing a parcel: there are the things lying around your room, the open carton you're filling, and the parcels you've already sent.

- The **working tree** is the files in your project folder, the ones you see and edit (your room).
- The **staging area** is a draft of your next commit (the open carton). You decide exactly what goes into it. Git's own commands sometimes call it the `index`.
- The history inside `.git` holds every commit you've made (the sent parcels). **`HEAD`** is Git's name for the commit you're on now, usually the latest one.

The everyday flow: edit files in the working tree, run `git add` to put the changes you want into the staging area, then run `git commit` to turn the staging area into a new, permanent commit.

Why the middle step? It lets you **shape** your commits. Say you fixed a mistake in one file and also tidied up two others. You can stage just the fix, commit it with a clear message, then stage and commit the tidying separately. Each commit then tells one clear story.

The same picture explains the two ways of looking at changes. Git shows changes as a **diff**: a listing of the lines removed and the lines added. `git diff` compares the working tree with the staging area, so it shows what you have *not* staged yet. `git diff --staged` compares the staging area with `HEAD`, so it shows what *will* go into the next commit.

Each file is in one of these states: **untracked** (Git has never been told about it), **unmodified** (same as in the last commit), **modified** (changed but not staged) or **staged**. `git status` tells you which files are in which state.
concepts.code:
echo "hello" > a.txt      # create a file containing the word hello
git status --short        # ?? a.txt   (untracked)
git add a.txt
git status --short        # A  a.txt   (staged)
git commit -m "Add a.txt"
echo "world" >> a.txt     # add a second line to the file
git status --short        #  M a.txt   (modified, not staged)
git diff                  # working tree vs staging area
git add a.txt
git diff --staged         # staging area vs HEAD: what the next commit contains
takeaways: Working tree -> git add -> staging area -> git commit -> history
The staging area is the draft of your next commit
git diff = changes not staged yet; git diff --staged = what you're about to commit
pitfalls: Editing a file again after git add and then committing — only the staged version goes in, not the later edit.

quiz.q: You edit app.py, run git add app.py, then edit app.py again and commit. What is committed?
options: The version as it was when you ran git add
Nothing, because the file changed after staging
quiz.explain: A commit records the staging area, which holds the content from the moment you ran git add.

quiz.q: Which command shows what the next commit will contain?
quiz.explain: --staged compares the staging area with HEAD, which is exactly what the commit would record.

concepts.name: Staging and committing
concepts.summary: Use git add to stage changes and git commit to save them as a commit with a clear message.
concepts.why: Commits are what history is made of; clear ones make changes easy to review, track down and undo.
concepts.body:
`git add <file>` copies the current content of a file into the staging area. That works for new files, changed files and, with `git add -A` or `git add .` (the dot means "this whole folder"), deleted files too. `git commit` then saves what is staged as a new commit, with a message.

Useful forms:

- `git add notes.txt docs/`: stage particular files or whole folders.
- `git add -p`: Git shows you each changed piece of each file in turn and asks `y` (stage it) or `n` (skip it). The best way to split unrelated changes into separate commits.
- `git commit -m "message"`: commit with a one-line message. Without `-m`, Git opens your text editor so you can write a longer one.
- `git commit -a`: stage every change to files Git already knows about, and commit, in one step. It skips brand-new files.
- `git commit --amend`: replace your last commit with a corrected one, to add a forgotten file or fix the message. Only do this before you've sent the commit to anyone else (sending is called *pushing*, covered soon).

A good commit is **one logical change** that leaves the project working. Write the message for a future reader: a short summary line of about 50 characters, phrased as an instruction ("Fix rounding in invoice totals"), then a blank line, then a few sentences on *why*, if that isn't obvious.

Every commit gets an ID that looks like `3f9a2c1...`. It's a **hash**: a fingerprint Git calculates from the commit's files, its message, its author and the commit before it. You can refer to a commit by the first 7 or so characters of its **commit ID**. Change anything about a commit, even one letter of its message, and you get a different ID. That's why amending a commit that others already have causes trouble.

Commit early and often. Small commits cost nothing, and they're far easier to understand and undo than one giant commit called "work in progress".
concepts.code:
git add src/invoice.py              # stage one file
git add -p                          # choose changed pieces one by one
git commit -m "Fix rounding in invoice totals"

# Longer message: a summary, then a second -m for the explanation
git commit -m "Cache exchange rates" -m "Rates were fetched per line item, making large invoices slow."

# Forgot a file? Add it to the last commit (only if not shared yet)
git add tests/test_invoice.py
git commit --amend --no-edit        # --no-edit: keep the same message

git log --oneline -3                # list the last 3 commits
# 9c1e2ab Cache exchange rates
# 3f9a2c1 Fix rounding in invoice totals
takeaways: git add stages; git commit saves what's staged as a new commit
git add -p lets you split unrelated edits into separate commits
One logical change per commit, with a short instruction-style summary
--amend replaces the last commit; don't amend commits you've shared
pitfalls: Expecting git commit -a to include brand-new files — it only stages files Git already tracks.

quiz.q: You created new.py and modified old.py. What does git commit -a -m 'x' commit?
quiz.explain: -a only stages changes to files Git already tracks; the untracked new.py is left out.

quiz.q: Why does git commit --amend change the commit's ID?
options: The ID is a hash of the commit's files, message, author and parent
Amend also deletes the parent commit
It doesn't; the ID stays the same
quiz.explain: The hash is calculated from the snapshot, message, author and previous commit, so any change gives a new ID.

concepts.name: Inspecting changes: status and diff
concepts.summary: Read git status and git diff to know exactly what changed before you commit.
concepts.why: Checking status and diff before every commit is the habit that prevents most accidental commits.
concepts.body:
`git status` is the command you'll run most. It tells you which branch you're on and lists files in three groups: changes staged for the next commit, changes not staged yet, and untracked files Git has never been told about. It also suggests the commands you're most likely to want next.

`git status -s` gives a short summary with two letters in front of each file. The left letter is about the staging area and the right one about the working tree: `M` modified, `A` added, `D` deleted, and `??` for untracked.

`git diff` shows the changed lines themselves. Lines starting with `-` were removed and lines starting with `+` were added. A line like `@@ -12,7 +12,8 @@` says where in the file each changed section sits (here, around line 12).

These forms differ only in *which two versions* they compare:

- `git diff`: working tree vs staging area (changes not staged yet).
- `git diff --staged` (also spelled `--cached`): staging area vs `HEAD` (what you're about to commit).
- `git diff HEAD`: working tree vs your last commit (everything you've changed).
- `git diff 3f9a2c1 HEAD`: an older commit vs your current one.

Handy extras: `--stat` prints a short per-file summary of how much changed, `--name-only` prints just the file names, and `-- notes.txt` (two dashes, then file names) limits the output to those files.

Make it a habit: `git status`, then `git diff --staged`, before every commit. It catches leftovers, such as a quick note to yourself, a stray file, or a password pasted into a settings file, before they enter history, where they are much harder to remove.
concepts.code:
git status
# On branch main
# Changes to be committed:   modified: app.py
# Changes not staged:        modified: README.md
# Untracked files:           notes.txt

git status -s
# M  app.py        <- staged
#  M README.md     <- modified, not staged
# ?? notes.txt     <- untracked

git diff --staged --stat          # app.py | 4 ++--
git diff 3f9a2c1 HEAD -- app.py   # one file: that older commit vs now
takeaways: git status: current branch, then staged / not staged / untracked files
The diff forms differ only in which two versions they compare
Check git status and git diff --staged before every commit
pitfalls: Running plain git diff after staging everything, seeing no output, and assuming there are no changes.

quiz.q: You staged all your edits. Which command still shows them?
quiz.explain: Once staged, the changes are in the staging area, so you compare it with HEAD using --staged.

quiz.q: In git status -s output ' M file.txt' (space, then M), what does it mean?
options: Modified in the working tree but not staged
quiz.explain: The left letter is about the staging area, the right one about the working tree; M on the right means changed but not staged.

concepts.name: Reading history with git log
concepts.summary: Browse, filter and search your project's history with git log, git show and git blame.
concepts.why: Understanding why a project is the way it is starts with reading its history.
concepts.body:
`git log` lists commits from newest to oldest, starting at `HEAD`. Its normal output is long; these forms are handier day to day:

- `git log --oneline`: one line per commit (short commit ID and summary).
- `git log --oneline --graph --all`: also draws a simple picture, made of text characters, of where branches split off and join again.
- `git log -p notes.txt`: every change ever made to one file, each with its diff.
- `git log -5`: only the five newest commits.

Filtering is where `log` gets powerful:

- `--author="Ada"`, `--since="2 weeks ago"`, `--until=2026-01-01`.
- `--grep="invoice"` searches commit messages.
- `-S "parse_date"` searches the changes themselves: it finds commits that added or removed that exact text. Perfect for "when did this line disappear?".

`git show <commit>` prints one commit: its author, date, message and diff. `git show <commit>:path/file` prints a file as it was in that commit.

`git blame file` labels every line of a file with the commit and author that last changed it. Use it to find the commit, then read that commit's message and diff for the *why*. `git blame -w` ignores changes that only added or removed spaces, and `-L 40,60` limits it to lines 40 to 60.

You can name a commit in several ways: its commit ID (or just the first few characters), a branch name, `HEAD`, or `HEAD~2`, meaning "two commits before `HEAD`".
concepts.code:
git log --oneline --graph --all -15
git log --author="Ada" --since="1 month ago" --oneline
git log -S "parse_date" --oneline        # when was this text added or removed?
git log --grep="invoice" --oneline       # commits whose message mentions invoice
git show 3f9a2c1                         # one commit with its diff
git show HEAD~2:src/app.py               # the file as it was 2 commits ago
git blame -w -L 40,60 src/app.py         # who last changed lines 40-60
takeaways: --oneline --graph --all gives a quick picture of the whole history
-S finds commits that add or remove some text; --grep searches messages
blame finds the commit; its message tells you why
HEAD~2 means two commits before the one you're on
pitfalls: Treating git blame as finding who's at fault — the last person to touch a line may only have tidied it; look further back.

quiz.q: Which command finds the commit that removed calls to legacy_auth()?
quiz.explain: -S searches the changes themselves for commits that add or remove that text; --grep only searches commit messages.

quiz.q: What does git show HEAD~2:notes.txt print?
options: The last two changes made to notes.txt
notes.txt as it was two commits before the current one
quiz.explain: HEAD~2 names the commit two steps back, and :notes.txt picks that file out of it.

concepts.name: Ignoring files with .gitignore
concepts.summary: Tell Git which files to leave out, such as passwords, downloaded add-ons and generated files, with a .gitignore file.
concepts.why: A tidy repository holds only the files people actually write; leaving out the rest avoids clutter and leaked passwords.
concepts.body:
Not every file in a project folder belongs in its history. Some are made automatically by programs, such as finished program files or short-lived notes a program writes while it runs. Some are downloaded add-ons the project uses, called **dependencies**, which anyone can download again. And some hold **secrets** such as passwords, which must never be shared.

A **`.gitignore`** file lists rules naming the files Git should act as if it can't see: they won't show up as untracked, and `git add .` skips them. It's an ordinary text file in your project folder. Commit it, so the whole team ignores the same files.

How the rules work:

- `*.log`: the `*` stands for "any characters", so this matches every file ending in `.log`, in any folder.
- `build/` (slash at the end): only folders named `build`, with everything inside them.
- `/config.local` (slash at the start): only that file next to the `.gitignore`, not in deeper folders.
- `**/tmp`: a `tmp` folder at any depth; `docs/**/*.pdf`: any PDF anywhere under `docs`.
- `!keep.log`: keep this file anyway, even though an earlier line ignored it. It can't rescue a file whose whole folder is ignored.
- Lines starting with `#` are notes for people; Git skips them.

A `.gitignore` can also sit in a subfolder, and then applies from there downward. For clutter only *you* create, such as files your editor leaves behind, use `.git/info/exclude` (this project only) or a personal ignore file set with `git config --global core.excludesFile`.

The big catch: **ignore rules only affect untracked files**. If a file is already committed, adding it to `.gitignore` changes nothing. Stop tracking it with `git rm --cached <file>` (which keeps your copy in the folder), then commit.

When a file is mysteriously ignored, `git check-ignore -v <file>` prints the exact `.gitignore` line responsible. Ready-made `.gitignore` files for most kinds of projects are collected at github.com/github/gitignore.
concepts.code:
# Write these lines into .gitignore (or just create the file in your editor)
cat > .gitignore <<'END'
# downloaded add-ons and build output
node_modules/
dist/
*.log
# local secrets, but keep the example file
.env*
!.env.example
END

git check-ignore -v dist/app.js
# .gitignore:3:dist/    dist/app.js

# Committed .env by mistake? Stop tracking it, keep the file
git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"
takeaways: Commit .gitignore so everyone ignores the same files
Ignore rules don't apply to files already tracked: use git rm --cached
git check-ignore -v explains why a path is ignored
pitfalls: Adding an already committed password file to .gitignore and assuming it's gone — it's still in the history, so change the password.

quiz.q: config.json is already committed. You add config.json to .gitignore and edit the file. What does git status show?
options: Nothing; the file is now ignored
quiz.explain: Once a file is tracked it stays tracked; ignore patterns only affect untracked files.

concepts.name: Remotes and remote-tracking branches
concepts.summary: A remote is a saved name for another copy of your repository; origin/main is your local note of where its main branch was.
concepts.why: Working together in Git means swapping commits between copies of a repository, and remotes are how you name those copies.
concepts.body:
A **remote** is a short name for another copy of your repository, usually one on a server or a hosting site, saved together with its URL. `git clone` creates one called `origin` automatically. In a repository you made with `git init`, you add it yourself: `git remote add origin <url>`. `git remote -v` lists them.

You can have several. When you contribute to someone else's project, it's common to make your own copy of it on the hosting site, called a **fork**, and keep two remotes: `origin` for your fork and `upstream` for the original project.

For each branch on a remote, Git keeps a **remote-tracking branch** such as `origin/main`. Think of it as a note in your own repository saying "last time I checked, `main` on `origin` was at this commit". It only changes when you talk to the remote with `git fetch` (download what's new), `git pull` or `git push`. It is not live: if a teammate adds commits, your `origin/main` won't show them until you fetch.

Your own `main` is a separate branch. Normally it is paired with `origin/main`, which is called its **upstream** branch. That pairing lets `git status` say "ahead 2, behind 1" (you have 2 commits they don't; they have 1 you don't), and lets a plain `git push` or `git pull` know where to go. `git branch -vv` shows each branch's upstream.

Other useful commands:

- `git remote show origin`: details about the remote's branches.
- `git remote rename` and `git remote remove`.
- `git remote set-url origin <new-url>`: when the repository gets a new address, or you switch from an `https://` address to an SSH one.

Remotes are just settings stored in `.git/config`; you can open that file to see exactly what's set up.
concepts.code:
git remote add origin git@github.com:me/notes.git
git remote add upstream https://github.com/team/notes.git
git remote -v
# origin    git@github.com:me/notes.git (fetch)
# origin    git@github.com:me/notes.git (push)
# upstream  https://github.com/team/notes.git (fetch) ...

git fetch upstream           # update your upstream/* notes
git branch -vv
# * main 3f9a2c1 [origin/main: ahead 2, behind 1] Fix totals
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/me/notes.git
takeaways: origin is just the default name clone gives the copy it came from
origin/main is a local note, updated only by fetch, pull or push
The upstream pairing powers ahead/behind counts and plain git push/pull
pitfalls: Believing origin/main reflects the server right now — run git fetch first.

quiz.q: A teammate pushed to main five minutes ago. You haven't fetched. What does your origin/main point to?
options: The state from your last fetch, pull or push
The same commit as your local main
quiz.explain: Remote-tracking branches only change when you talk to the remote (fetch, pull or push).

concepts.name: Sharing work: push and pull
concepts.summary: Upload your commits with git push and bring in others' commits with git pull.
concepts.why: These two commands are the everyday routine of working together through a shared repository.
concepts.body:
**`git push`** uploads your new commits to a branch on a remote. The first time you push a new branch, add `-u` to make the remote branch its upstream, so later pushes and pulls need nothing extra:

```bash
git push -u origin feature-login
```

A push is only accepted if it simply *adds* commits on top of what the remote branch already has. That kind of update is called a **fast-forward**. If a teammate pushed first, the remote has commits you don't, and Git rejects yours: "Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally". The fix is to bring their work in first, then push again.

**`git pull`** does that: it downloads new commits from the upstream and combines them with your branch. When you both have new commits, there are two ways to combine them. A **merge** keeps both lines of work and ties them together with one extra commit.

The other way is a **rebase**: Git lifts your new commits off, then replays them on top of your teammate's, as if you had started after them. Both are covered properly later. Recent Git versions refuse to guess, so set `pull.rebase` once in your settings. Many people choose `pull.rebase true`, which keeps the history a straight line.

The everyday routine on a shared branch:

- `git pull` to start from the latest state.
- Edit, `git add`, `git commit`.
- `git pull` again if time has passed.
- `git push`.

If you and a teammate changed the same lines, the pull stops and asks you to decide what the result should be. That's a **merge conflict**, and a later lesson shows how to resolve one.

**Never** use `git push --force` to get past a rejection: it replaces the remote branch with yours and wipes out your teammates' new commits. If you truly need to replace a branch only you use (after a rebase, say), use `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if anyone has pushed since you last looked.
concepts.code:
git push -u origin main          # first push: set the upstream
# ... later
git commit -am "Update docs"
git push
# ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)

git pull --rebase                # bring in their commits, replay mine on top
git push                         # now it only adds commits: accepted

git config --global pull.rebase true   # make --rebase the default
takeaways: push -u once per new branch; afterwards just git push
A push may only add commits on top; a rejection means pull first
pull = download + merge or rebase; set pull.rebase to choose
Prefer --force-with-lease over --force, and never force a shared branch
pitfalls: Answering a rejected push with git push --force and silently deleting a teammate's commits.

quiz.q: Your push is rejected because the remote has commits you don't have. What is the right next step?
options: Delete your local branch and re-clone
git pull (merge or rebase), then push
quiz.explain: Combine the remote's commits with yours first, so your push only adds on top (a fast-forward).

quiz.q: What does --force-with-lease add over --force?
options: It only overwrites if the remote is still where you last saw it
It asks the server administrator for approval
It creates a backup branch on the server
quiz.explain: It refuses if someone pushed since you last fetched, so you can't wipe out work you haven't seen.

concepts.name: Branches
concepts.summary: A branch is a movable label on a commit; create, switch and delete branches freely with git switch and git branch.
concepts.why: Branches let you develop features and fixes in isolation without disturbing working code.
concepts.body:
In Git a **branch** is nothing more than a tiny file holding one commit ID: a label stuck on that commit. When you commit on a branch, its label moves forward to the new commit. **`HEAD`** says which branch you are on, so Git knows which label to move.

Because branches are just labels, creating one is instant and costs nothing. That's why people make a new branch for every feature, fix and experiment.

The modern commands (Git 2.23 and newer):

- `git switch -c feature-x`: create a branch at the current commit and switch to it.
- `git switch main`: switch back. The files in your working tree change to match that branch's latest commit.
- `git switch -c fix origin/fix`: create a local branch from a remote one (plain `git switch fix` does this automatically if exactly one remote has a branch called `fix`).
- `git branch`: list local branches; `-a` includes remote-tracking ones; `-vv` shows upstreams.
- `git branch -d feature-x`: delete a branch whose work is already merged; `-D` forces deletion of an unmerged one.
- `git branch -m new-name`: rename the current branch.

The older `git checkout` does all of this too, plus restoring files, which is why `switch` and `restore` were split out of it; you'll still see `checkout` in many tutorials.

Switching with uncommitted changes works if they don't clash with the branch you're switching to; otherwise Git refuses rather than lose your work. Commit first, or set the changes aside with `git stash` (covered soon).

If you switch to a specific commit instead of a branch (`git switch --detach 3f9a2c1`), you are in **detached HEAD**: `HEAD` points straight at a commit, not at a branch. New commits made there belong to no branch, so create one with `git switch -c` if you want to keep them.
concepts.code:
git switch -c feature/login        # create + switch
echo "form" > login.html
git add login.html && git commit -m "Add login form"
git switch main                     # login.html disappears from disk
git branch -vv
#   feature/login 7d1c0aa Add login form
# * main          3f9a2c1 [origin/main] Fix totals
git log --oneline --graph --all
git branch -d feature/login         # error: not fully merged
git branch -D feature/login         # force delete
takeaways: A branch is a movable label on a commit; HEAD names the current branch
git switch -c creates and switches; git branch -d deletes merged branches
Detached HEAD: commits made there need a branch to be kept
pitfalls: Doing work in detached HEAD and switching away — those commits belong to no branch and are hard to find again.

quiz.q: What actually happens on disk when you create a branch?
options: All files are copied into a new folder
A small file naming the current commit is created
quiz.explain: Creating a branch writes one small file containing a commit ID, which is why it's instant.

quiz.q: You commit while on branch feature. What moves?
options: The feature pointer, to the new commit
quiz.explain: The branch HEAD is on moves to the new commit; HEAD still names that branch.

concepts.name: Merging branches
concepts.summary: Combine branches with git merge, and know when Git fast-forwards and when it creates a merge commit.
concepts.why: Merging is how finished work lands on main; knowing the two kinds keeps history readable.
concepts.body:
`git merge <branch>` brings the commits of `<branch>` into the branch you are on. There are two outcomes.

**Fast-forward**: if your current branch hasn't moved since `<branch>` was created, its commits simply sit on top of yours. Git just moves your branch label forward; no new commit is made and history stays a straight line.

**Three-way merge**: if both branches have new commits, Git finds their **merge base**: the last commit both branches share, where they split apart. It compares each side with that commit to see what each changed, and combines the changes. It records the result as a **merge commit**, a commit with two previous commits (called *parents*) instead of one. Changes to different files, or different parts of the same file, combine automatically; edits to the same lines become merge conflicts (next lesson).

You can control which you get:

- `git merge --no-ff feature` always creates a merge commit, even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the fact that a group of commits was one feature.
- `git merge --ff-only feature` refuses unless a fast-forward is possible. Good for updating a local `main` from `origin/main` without accidental merges.
- `git merge --squash feature` stages the combined changes as one new commit you then create, without recording the branch as merged.

After merging, delete the feature branch with `git branch -d`; its commits are safe in `main`'s history. `git branch --merged` lists branches already merged into the current one, handy for cleanup.

Merge never rewrites existing commits. That makes it safe on shared branches, at the price of merge commits in the graph.
concepts.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/login            # Fast-forward (main hadn't moved)

git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/search -m "Merge search feature"
git log --oneline --graph -5
# *   b4e7d21 Merge search feature
# |\
# | * 91aa3c0 Add search index
# * | 3f9a2c1 Fix totals
# |/
git branch --merged                # safe-to-delete branches
git branch -d feature/search
takeaways: Fast-forward just moves the branch label; three-way merge makes a two-parent commit
The merge base is the shared commit Git compares both sides against
--no-ff keeps feature grouping; --ff-only refuses real merges
Merging never rewrites existing commits
pitfalls: Using --squash and then deleting the branch with -d — Git doesn't consider it merged, so -d refuses; that's expected.

quiz.q: main has not moved since feature branched off. What does git merge feature (on main) do by default?
options: Creates a merge commit with two parents
quiz.explain: With no divergent commits, Git just moves the main pointer forward.

quiz.q: Which commit does Git use as the reference point in a three-way merge?
options: The merge base, the best common ancestor
The first commit in the repository
The most recent commit by date
quiz.explain: Both sides are compared against their common ancestor to work out who changed what.

concepts.name: Resolving merge conflicts
concepts.summary: When both sides change the same lines, edit the conflict markers, git add the result and conclude the merge.
concepts.why: Conflicts are routine in team work; resolving them calmly and correctly is a core skill.
concepts.body:
A **conflict** happens when both branches changed the same lines (or one edited a file the other deleted) since the merge base. Git stops mid-merge, merges everything it can, and marks the rest. `git status` lists the files under "Unmerged paths".

Inside a conflicted file you will see:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
total = round(sum(items), 2)
=======
total = sum(items).quantize(CENT)
>>>>>>> feature/decimal
```

The top part is your current branch (`HEAD`), the bottom is the incoming branch. Your job is to edit the file into what the code **should** be, which might be one side, the other, or a combination, and delete all markers. Then:

- `git add <file>` to mark it resolved.
- When all files are resolved, `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) to create the merge commit.

Tips that make conflicts easier:

- Set `git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3`. Markers then also show the **base** version (`|||||||`), so you can see what each side actually changed.
- `git checkout --ours file` or `--theirs file` takes one side wholesale for a file.
- `git mergetool` opens a visual comparison tool you have set up; most code editors can also show conflicts with buttons to pick a side.
- If the project has automated tests (small programs that check it still works), run them before committing: a merge with no conflicts can still produce something broken.

If it goes wrong, `git merge --abort` returns you to the state before the merge. The same markers appear in other commands you will meet (`git rebase`, `git cherry-pick`, `git stash pop`), where you continue with that command's `--continue` instead.
concepts.code:
git merge feature/decimal
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in billing.py
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
git status --short
# UU billing.py
$EDITOR billing.py                     # remove markers, write the right code
grep -n '<<<<<<<\|>>>>>>>' billing.py  # make sure none are left
git add billing.py
python -m pytest -q                    # run the tests: still works?
git merge --continue                   # creates the merge commit

# Or bail out entirely
git merge --abort
takeaways: Conflict = both sides changed the same region since the merge base
Edit to the correct result, remove markers, git add, then continue
zdiff3 conflict style shows the base version too
git merge --abort returns to the pre-merge state
pitfalls: Committing a file that still contains <<<<<<< markers.
Blindly taking --ours or --theirs without reading what the other side changed.

quiz.q: During a merge on main of feature, what is between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======?
options: The version from main, the branch you are on
quiz.explain: HEAD is the current branch; the incoming branch's version follows the ======= line.

quiz.q: How do you tell Git a conflicted file is resolved?
quiz.explain: Staging the file marks it resolved; once all are staged, conclude the merge.

concepts.name: Fetch vs pull
concepts.summary: git fetch downloads new commits without touching your branches; git pull fetches and then merges or rebases.
concepts.why: Fetching first lets you see what changed before it lands in your work.
concepts.body:
**`git fetch`** contacts a remote, downloads any commits you don't have, and updates the remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`, `origin/feature-x`...). It never changes your local branches or working tree, so it is always safe to run.

**`git pull`** is `git fetch` followed by integrating the upstream of your current branch into it, by merge or rebase depending on `pull.rebase` or the flags `--rebase` / `--no-rebase` / `--ff-only`.

Fetching separately gives you a chance to look before you leap:

```bash
git fetch
git log --oneline main..origin/main    # what's new upstream
git diff main...origin/main            # what they changed
```

Two dots, `main..origin/main`, means "commits on `origin/main` that aren't on `main`"; three dots in `git diff` mean "changes on `origin/main` since the two split apart". Then integrate deliberately: `git merge origin/main`, `git rebase origin/main`, or `git merge --ff-only origin/main` if you have no local commits.

Some options worth knowing:

- `git fetch --all` fetches every remote.
- `git fetch --prune` (or `fetch.prune true` in config) deletes remote-tracking branches whose branch was deleted on the server, so `git branch -r` doesn't fill up with ghosts.
- `git pull --ff-only` is a safe default for a branch you never commit to directly, such as a local `main`: it updates if possible and refuses otherwise.

A good mental model: fetch updates your *knowledge* of the remote; merge or rebase changes *your* branch. `git pull` simply does both at once, which is convenient when you already know what to expect.
concepts.code:
git fetch --prune origin
git status
# Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 3 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main     # the 3 incoming commits
git merge --ff-only origin/main          # same result as git pull --ff-only

git config --global fetch.prune true
git pull --rebase                        # fetch + rebase in one step
takeaways: fetch only updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main; it never touches your work
pull = fetch + merge/rebase into the current branch
Fetch, inspect with main..origin/main, then integrate on purpose
fetch.prune cleans up remote branches deleted on the server

quiz.q: You run git fetch and the remote had 5 new commits on main. What changed locally?
options: Your main branch now has the 5 commits
origin/main moved; your main and files are unchanged
quiz.explain: Fetch only downloads commits and moves remote-tracking branches such as origin/main.

quiz.q: Which command shows commits that are on origin/main but not yet on your main?
quiz.explain: A..B lists commits reachable from B (origin/main) but not from A (main).

concepts.name: Undoing changes: restore and reset
concepts.summary: Discard edits, unstage files and move a branch back to an earlier commit with git restore and git reset.
concepts.why: Knowing exactly what each undo command touches is what makes Git feel safe instead of scary.
concepts.body:
Undo commands differ in which of the three areas (working tree, staging area, `HEAD`) they change.

**`git restore`** works on files:

- `git restore file`: throw away changes you haven't staged, copying the staging area's version back into the working tree. Those edits are gone for good.
- `git restore --staged file`: unstage, copying `HEAD`'s version into the staging area; your edits stay in the file.
- `git restore --source=HEAD~3 file`: bring back an older version of a file.

**`git reset <commit>`** moves the current **branch** back (or forward) to another commit, then optionally updates the other areas:

- `--soft`: move the branch only. The changes from the undone commits stay staged. Handy to **squash** (combine) the last few commits into one.
- `--mixed` (the default): also reset the staging area. The changes stay in your files, unstaged.
- `--hard`: also reset the working tree. Uncommitted changes are **destroyed**.

So `git reset --soft HEAD~1` "uncommits" the last commit but keeps its work staged, and `git reset --hard origin/main` throws away everything local to match the remote.

Reset rewrites the branch's history: the commits after the new position are no longer on the branch. (Git can still find them for a while through its reflog, a recovery log covered in a later lesson.) That's fine for commits only you have. But if they've been pushed, others still have them, and your next push would need force. For shared history, use `git revert`, covered next.

Before any `--hard`, run `git status`, and commit anything you might want (or set it aside with `git stash`).
concepts.code:
git restore config.yml               # throw away unstaged edits
git restore --staged secrets.txt     # unstage, keep the file as is
git restore --source=v1.4 -- api.py  # old version of one file

git reset --soft HEAD~3              # undo 3 commits, keep changes staged
git commit -m "Add search (squashed)"

git reset HEAD~1                     # --mixed: uncommit + unstage, keep edits
git reset --hard origin/main         # discard ALL local commits and edits
takeaways: restore = files; reset = move the branch to another commit
--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstaged, --hard deletes them
Reset only commits you haven't shared; use revert for pushed ones
pitfalls: Running git reset --hard with uncommitted work you wanted — work that was never committed can't be recovered.

quiz.q: You want to undo your last (unpushed) commit but keep its changes staged to recommit them. Which command?
quiz.explain: --soft moves only the branch, leaving the staging area and working tree as they were.

quiz.q: What does git restore --staged app.py do to your edits in app.py?
options: Keeps them in the file but removes them from the staging area
Moves them to a new branch
quiz.explain: --staged copies HEAD's version into the staging area; the file in the working tree is untouched.

concepts.name: Reverting commits safely
concepts.summary: git revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one, without rewriting shared history.
concepts.why: It's the correct way to back out a bad change that others have already pulled.
concepts.body:
**`git revert <commit>`** works out the opposite of a commit's changes (lines it added are removed, lines it removed come back) and records that as a **new commit**, by default with a message like `Revert "Add caching layer"`. The original commit stays in history; the branch simply moves forward.

Because nothing is rewritten, revert is safe on `main` and any branch others use. Compare with `git reset`, which moves the branch backwards and forces everyone else to deal with commits disappearing.

Useful forms:

- `git revert HEAD`: undo the most recent commit.
- `git revert a1b2c3d e4f5a6b`: several commits, each reverted in its own new commit.
- `git revert --no-commit A..B` (or `-n`): undo a whole range (the commits after `A`, up to and including `B`) in your files and staging area, then commit once.

If later commits changed the same lines, the revert can **conflict**; resolve it like any other conflict, then `git revert --continue` (or `--abort`).

Reverting a **merge commit** needs `-m 1` to say which parent is the mainline you want to keep, usually parent 1 (the branch you merged into). Beware a subtle consequence: Git now considers the feature's commits merged *and* undone, so merging that branch again later won't re-apply them. To bring the feature back, revert the revert.

In practice, revert is how teams quickly undo a change that broke the live product: revert, push, release again, then fix the real problem calmly in a follow-up commit.
concepts.code:
git log --oneline -4
# e9f0b12 Add caching layer     <- broke the live site
# 3f9a2c1 Fix totals
git revert e9f0b12 --no-edit
# [main 5c7d8e9] Revert "Add caching layer"
git push                          # normal push, no force needed

# Undo a merge, keeping the mainline (parent 1)
git revert -m 1 b4e7d21

# Bring the feature back later
git revert 5c7d8e9
takeaways: Revert adds a new inverse commit; history is not rewritten
Safe for pushed/shared branches, unlike reset
Merge commits need -m 1 to choose the mainline parent
pitfalls: Re-merging a feature branch after reverting its merge and expecting the changes back — revert the revert instead.

quiz.q: A bad commit is already on the shared main branch. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: Delete the commit on the hosting site
git revert the commit and push
quiz.explain: Revert adds a new commit, so collaborators' history stays valid.

concepts.name: Stashing work in progress
concepts.summary: Save uncommitted changes aside with git stash, switch context, and reapply them later.
concepts.why: Interruptions happen; stash lets you switch branches without committing half-done work.
concepts.body:
**`git stash`** takes your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged edits to tracked files), saves them in a list of stashes (newest first), and resets your working tree to match `HEAD`. You get a clean tree to switch branches, pull or test something, then bring the changes back.

Commands:

- `git stash push -m "wip: search"`: stash with a description (plain `git stash` works too).
- `git stash -u`: also stash **untracked** files, which are left behind by default.
- `git stash list`: shows `stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`... newest first.
- `git stash show -p stash@{1}`: see what's in one.
- `git stash pop`: apply the newest stash and drop it if it applied cleanly.
- `git stash apply stash@{1}`: apply without dropping, so you can apply it elsewhere too.
- `git stash drop stash@{1}` / `git stash clear`: delete.
- `git stash branch new-branch`: create a branch at the commit you stashed from and apply it there, which avoids conflicts when the original branch has moved on.

A stash can be applied on any branch, which makes it a quick way to move uncommitted edits you started on the wrong branch. Applying can conflict; if `pop` conflicts, the stash is **kept**, so after resolving you drop it yourself.

Stashes are easy to forget, and an old stash is hard to understand. For anything longer than a quick interruption, prefer a work-in-progress commit on a branch, or a second working folder (`git worktree`, an advanced lesson).
concepts.code:
# Mid-feature, an urgent bug report arrives
git stash push -u -m "wip: search filters"
git switch main && git switch -c hotfix/login
# ... fix, commit, push ...
git switch feature/search
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feature/search: wip: search filters
git stash pop                   # changes are back, stash dropped

# Started on the wrong branch? Move edits over
git stash && git switch correct-branch && git stash pop
takeaways: stash saves tracked changes and cleans the tree; -u includes untracked files
pop = apply + drop; apply keeps the stash
A conflicting pop keeps the stash so nothing is lost
pitfalls: Forgetting -u, switching branches, and finding new untracked files have followed you.

quiz.q: You ran git stash with a brand-new, never-added file in the folder. Where is that file afterwards?
options: Still in the working tree, untouched
quiz.explain: Untracked files are only stashed with -u (or -a for ignored files too).

concepts.name: Rebasing a branch
concepts.summary: git rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history; never rebase shared commits.
concepts.why: Rebase keeps feature branches current and history clean, but misused it rewrites others' work.
concepts.body:
Suppose you branched `feature` from `main`, made three commits, and `main` has moved on. Merging would add a merge commit. **`git rebase main`** (run on `feature`) instead takes your three commits, sets them aside, moves `feature` to the tip of `main`, and **replays** each commit on top, one by one.

The result looks as if you had started your work from today's `main`: a straight line, no merge commit, and a later merge into `main` becomes a fast-forward.

The catch: replayed commits are **new commits** with new IDs, because their parent changed. The old ones are abandoned. Hence the **golden rule: don't rebase commits that others have based work on.** Rebasing your own unpublished, or personal pushed, branch is fine; you'll then need `git push --force-with-lease` to update the remote copy.

Conflicts are resolved per replayed commit:

- Fix the files, `git add` them, then `git rebase --continue`.
- `git rebase --skip` drops the current commit; `git rebase --abort` returns everything to how it was before you started.

Merge or rebase? Both are valid; teams pick a convention. Merge preserves exactly what happened; rebase produces a history that is easier to read and search. A common combination is rebasing your feature branch onto `main` to stay current, and merging it into `main` once it has been reviewed.

`git pull --rebase` is the same idea for your local commits versus newly fetched upstream ones.
concepts.code:
git switch feature/search
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/search.

# On conflict:
#   edit files, then
git add search.py
git rebase --continue      # or --skip / --abort

git log --oneline --graph -5          # linear on top of origin/main
git push --force-with-lease           # branch was pushed before: update it
takeaways: Rebase replays your commits on a new base, producing new commit IDs
Golden rule: don't rebase commits others have built on
Resolve per commit: git add, then git rebase --continue
After rebasing a pushed branch, use --force-with-lease
pitfalls: Rebasing main (or any shared branch) onto something else and force-pushing — everyone else's history breaks.

quiz.q: Why do commits get new IDs after a rebase?
options: Their parent commit changed, and the parent is part of the hash
quiz.explain: A commit's ID is calculated partly from its parent's ID, so a new starting point means new commits.

quiz.q: Mid-rebase you realize it's a mess. What gets you back to the exact pre-rebase state?
quiz.explain: --abort restores the branch to where it was before the rebase started.

concepts.name: Pull request workflow
concepts.summary: Push a feature branch, open a pull request, get review and automatic checks, then merge using your team's chosen style.
concepts.why: Pull requests are how almost every team reviews changes and gets them into main.
concepts.body:
A **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request) is a feature of hosting sites, not a Git command. It asks to merge one branch into another, and comes with a page on the website for discussion, review and automatic checks. Underneath, it is still branches and commits.

The typical routine:

- Update `main`, then `git switch -c feature/x`.
- Make focused commits; push with `git push -u origin feature/x`.
- Open the PR on the website, or with `gh pr create` (a GitHub program you use from the terminal). Describe *what* changed and *why*, how to test it, and link the issue (the task or problem report) it addresses.
- Automatic checks run the project's tests on the branch. This setup is called **CI**, short for continuous integration. Meanwhile teammates read the changes and comment.
- Answer feedback with new commits and push again; the PR updates by itself.
- If `main` moved on and conflicts appear, merge or rebase `origin/main` into your branch and push.
- Merge, then delete the branch, both locally and on the remote.

Hosting sites offer three merge buttons, and teams usually pick one:

- **Merge commit**: keeps every commit plus a merge commit.
- **Squash and merge**: the whole PR is squashed (combined) into one commit on `main`. Clean history, but the individual commits are lost.
- **Rebase and merge**: replays the commits onto `main` in a straight line.

For **open-source** projects (public projects that anyone may copy and contribute to) you usually can't push to the original repository. So you fork it, push branches to your fork (`origin`) and open PRs against the original (`upstream`).

Keep PRs small. A 200-line PR gets a careful review in minutes; a 2,000-line one gets a quick "looks good to me".
concepts.code:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feature/rate-limit
# ... commits ...
git push -u origin feature/rate-limit
gh pr create --title "Add rate limiting" --body "Limits /api to 100 req/min. Closes #42."

# Reviewer asked for changes
git commit -am "Address review: make limit configurable"
git push                                   # PR updates

# After merge on the platform
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feature/rate-limit
git push origin --delete feature/rate-limit  # if not auto-deleted
takeaways: A PR is a platform feature around merging one branch into another
Push new commits to the same branch to update a PR
Merge, squash or rebase: pick one team convention
Fork + upstream remote for projects you can't push to
pitfalls: Piling unrelated changes into one PR — split them; reviewing and undoing both get easier.

quiz.q: A reviewer requests changes on your open PR. How do you update it?
options: Close it and open a new PR
Commit the fixes and push to the same branch
Email a patch to the reviewer
Push the fixes directly to main
quiz.explain: The PR tracks the branch, so new pushes to it appear automatically.

quiz.q: What does 'squash and merge' put on main?
options: Every commit from the PR plus a merge commit
A single commit containing all the PR's changes
quiz.explain: Squashing combines the PR's changes into one new commit on the target branch.

concepts.name: Tagging releases
concepts.summary: Mark release points with annotated tags, push them, and use git describe to name versions.
concepts.why: Tags give permanent, human-readable names to the exact commits you shipped.
concepts.body:
A **tag** is a name for a specific commit that, unlike a branch, does not move. Tags mark releases (`v2.4.0`), so you can always check out, diff against or rebuild exactly what shipped.

There are two kinds:

- **Lightweight** (`git tag v1.0`): just a name pointing at a commit, like a branch that never moves.
- **Annotated** (`git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0"`): a full record with who made it, the date and a message, and optionally a digital signature (`-s`) proving who made it. Use annotated tags for releases; `git describe` and most release tools expect them.

Tags are **not pushed by default**. Push one with `git push origin v1.0`, all with `git push --tags`, or set `push.followTags true` so `git push` also sends annotated tags on the commits you push.

Other commands:

- `git tag -l "v2.*"`: list matching tags.
- `git show v1.0`: the tag message and the commit.
- `git tag -a v0.9 3f9a2c1 -m "..."`: tag an older commit.
- `git tag -d v1.0` then `git push origin --delete v1.0`: delete locally and remotely.

`git describe` names any commit relative to the nearest annotated tag, for example `v2.4.0-12-g9c1e2ab` = 12 commits after v2.4.0, at commit `9c1e2ab`. Many projects show this as the version number of their software.

Treat published tags as permanent. Moving a release tag after people have fetched it leads to confusing mismatches; make a new version instead.
concepts.code:
git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0"
git push origin v2.4.0
git config --global push.followTags true   # push annotated tags with commits

git tag -l "v2.*"           # v2.3.0  v2.4.0
git describe                # v2.4.0-12-g9c1e2ab
git switch --detach v2.3.0  # look at an old release
git diff v2.3.0 v2.4.0 --stat
takeaways: Tags are fixed names for commits; branches move, tags don't
Use annotated tags (-a or -s) for releases
Tags aren't pushed by default: push them or enable push.followTags
Don't move published tags; release a new version
pitfalls: Tagging locally and forgetting to push the tag, so the automated release steps never see it.

quiz.q: You created tag v1.2 and ran git push. Does the remote have the tag?
options: Yes, all tags are always pushed
Yes, but only if it is lightweight
No, unless you push it explicitly or enable push.followTags
quiz.explain: Plain git push sends branches; tags need to be pushed explicitly or via followTags.

concepts.name: Interactive rebase
concepts.summary: Reorder, squash, reword, split or drop commits with git rebase -i before sharing them.
concepts.why: Turning a messy series of work-in-progress commits into a clean, reviewable story is what interactive rebase is for.
concepts.body:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens your editor with a **todo list** of every commit after `<base>`, oldest first. Each line starts with a command; you edit the list, save, and Git replays the commits accordingly:

- `pick`: keep the commit as is.
- `reword`: keep it but edit the message.
- `edit`: stop after applying it so you can amend it or split it into several commits.
- `squash`: meld into the previous commit and combine the messages.
- `fixup`: meld into the previous commit and discard this message (`fixup -C` keeps this one's message instead).
- `drop` (or delete the line): remove the commit.
- `exec <cmd>`: run a command at that point, for example the project's tests; the rebase stops if it fails.

Reordering lines reorders commits. Typical use: `git rebase -i origin/main` to tidy everything your branch adds before asking others to review it.

**Autosquash** saves editing by hand. When you notice a mistake in an earlier commit, fix it and run `git commit --fixup=<that-commit>`. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main` (or `rebase.autoSquash true`) moves each fixup under its target, already marked.

To split a commit: mark it `edit`; when Git stops, run `git reset HEAD~`, then stage and commit pieces separately, then `git rebase --continue`.

If you stack branches (`part1` on which `part2` is built), `--update-refs` moves those in-between branch labels along too.

All the usual rebase rules apply: new commit IDs, so only rewrite commits not yet shared, and `git rebase --abort` gets you out at any point.
concepts.code:
git commit --fixup=3f9a2c1          # "fixup! Add search index"
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
# Editor shows (oldest first):
#   pick   3f9a2c1 Add search index
#   fixup  a77b1e0 fixup! Add search index
#   pick   5d2e9f1 WIP
#   pick   8c4b0aa Add search UI
# Change to:
#   pick   3f9a2c1 Add search index
#   fixup  a77b1e0 fixup! Add search index
#   squash 5d2e9f1 WIP
#   reword 8c4b0aa Add search UI
#   exec   make test
git push --force-with-lease
takeaways: The todo list is oldest-first; reorder lines to reorder commits
squash merges messages; fixup discards the fixup's message
commit --fixup + rebase --autosquash automates cleanup
exec runs tests at any point in the replay
pitfalls: Interactive-rebasing commits already merged into a shared branch, creating duplicate commits for everyone.

quiz.q: What is the difference between squash and fixup in the todo list?
options: squash combines messages; fixup keeps only the earlier commit's message
fixup deletes the changes; squash keeps them
squash works only on the first commit
quiz.explain: Both meld changes into the previous commit; fixup throws away its own message.

quiz.q: In which order does git rebase -i list commits?
options: Oldest first, in the order they will be replayed
quiz.explain: The todo list is a replay script, so it starts from the oldest commit after the base.

concepts.name: Cherry-picking commits
concepts.summary: Apply the changes of specific commits onto your current branch with git cherry-pick.
concepts.why: Backporting a fix to a release branch, or rescuing one commit from an abandoned branch, is a cherry-pick.
concepts.body:
**`git cherry-pick <commit>`** takes the diff a commit introduced and applies it as a **new commit** on your current branch, with the same message and author. The original stays where it was; the copy gets a new ID.

The classic use is **backporting**: copying a fix to an older version people still use. A problem was fixed on `main`, and you need the same fix on `release/2.3`, a **release branch** kept for version 2.3. You switch to the release branch and cherry-pick the fix commit.

Variants:

- `git cherry-pick A B C`: several commits, applied in order.
- `git cherry-pick A..B`: a range, excluding `A` itself (use `A^..B` to include it; `A^` means the commit before `A`).
- `-x` appends "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message. Use it for backports so the link is traceable.
- `-n` / `--no-commit` applies changes without committing, so you can combine several picks into one commit.
- `-m 1` picks a merge commit relative to its first parent.

Conflicts are handled like in rebase: fix, `git add`, `git cherry-pick --continue`; or `--skip` / `--abort`.

Use it sparingly. Cherry-picked copies are separate commits, so if both branches are later merged, Git sees the same change twice. Usually it merges cleanly, but it can produce confusing conflicts, and `git log` shows the change twice. Prefer merging the fix branch into both places when your workflow allows it; cherry-pick is for situations where merging would bring in too much.

`git log --cherry-pick --oneline A...B` hides commits whose changes appear on both sides, useful for spotting what was already backported.
concepts.code:
git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 7e1f3c2
# [release/2.3 4a9b0d1] Fix null check in parser
#  (cherry picked from commit 7e1f3c2...)

git cherry-pick main~5..main~2     # 3 commits: main~4, main~3, main~2
# CONFLICT in parser.py
git add parser.py
git cherry-pick --continue

# What on main is not yet on release (ignoring equivalent picks)?
git log --oneline --cherry-pick --right-only release/2.3...main
takeaways: cherry-pick copies a commit's change as a new commit on the current branch
A..B excludes A; use A^..B to include it
Use -x for backports so the origin is recorded
pitfalls: Using cherry-pick as the normal way to move work between long-lived branches — duplicate commits make later merges confusing.

quiz.q: What does git cherry-pick X..Y apply?
options: Commits after X up to and including Y
Commits from X up to but not including Y
quiz.explain: Range syntax excludes the left endpoint, so X itself is not picked.

concepts.name: Reflog and recovering lost work
concepts.summary: The reflog records every position HEAD and your branches have had, so you can undo resets, bad rebases and deleted branches.
concepts.why: It turns 'I destroyed my work' into a two-minute fix, which makes you braver with history rewriting.
concepts.body:
Every time `HEAD` or a branch moves (commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge, amend, pull), Git appends an entry to the **reflog**. It's local only, never pushed, and it is your undo history.

`git reflog` shows `HEAD`'s log, newest first:

```text
9d2c4e1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
5b7a0f3 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export button
...
```

`HEAD@{1}` means "where HEAD was one move ago". `git reflog show feature` shows a branch's own log, and time-based forms such as `main@{yesterday}` work too.

Recovery recipes:

- **Undo a bad reset or rebase**: find the entry from before it, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{4}` (or the hash). After a rebase, `ORIG_HEAD` also points at the pre-rebase tip.
- **Restore a deleted branch**: find its last commit in the reflog (`git branch -D` prints the hash too) and `git branch feature <hash>`.
- **Rescue commits made in detached HEAD** (while no branch was checked out): they are in `HEAD`'s reflog; create a branch at them.

Commits removed from all branches are **unreachable** (no branch or tag leads to them) but not deleted immediately. Reflog entries expire after 90 days by default (30 days for entries no longer reachable), and Git's clean-up command, `git gc`, then deletes those commits. If even the reflog is gone, `git fsck --lost-found` can find commits that nothing points to.

The limit: the reflog tracks **commits**. Changes you never committed or stashed, then wiped with `reset --hard` or `restore`, are not in it. Commit often and you can always get back.
concepts.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~3          # oops, those commits mattered
git reflog -5
# 9d2c4e1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 5b7a0f3 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export button
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}        # back to before the reset

git branch -D experiment         # Deleted branch experiment (was 41c8e2a).
git branch experiment 41c8e2a    # restored

git rebase origin/main           # went wrong?
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD       # tip before the rebase
takeaways: Every HEAD/branch movement is logged locally in the reflog
Recover with git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git branch name <hash>
Unreachable commits survive about 30-90 days before Git's clean-up deletes them
Uncommitted work is not in the reflog
pitfalls: Expecting the reflog to exist on a fresh clone — it's local to each repository.

quiz.q: You hard-reset away three commits an hour ago. Can you get them back?
options: Yes, find them in git reflog and reset or branch to them
quiz.explain: The commits are still stored, and the reflog recorded where HEAD was.

quiz.q: Which of these can the reflog NOT recover?
options: A branch deleted with git branch -D
Commits lost in a bad rebase
Edits never committed or stashed, discarded with git restore
quiz.explain: The reflog records commits HEAD pointed to; uncommitted edits never became commits.

concepts.name: Finding bugs with git bisect
concepts.summary: Find the exact commit that introduced a bug by testing the halfway point again and again with git bisect, by hand or with a script.
concepts.why: It finds the culprit among thousands of commits in a dozen steps, often fully automatically.
concepts.body:
When something worked in `v2.3.0` and is broken now, the **bug** (a mistake that makes the program behave wrongly) was introduced by one commit in between. **`git bisect`** searches that range by halving it: it checks out the commit in the middle, you say whether it's good or bad, and it throws away the half that can't contain the culprit. 1,000 commits take about 10 steps.

The manual flow:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # current commit is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0      # this one was fine
```

Git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. Repeat until Git prints "<hash> is the first bad commit". `git bisect reset` returns you to where you started.

If a commit can't be tested (it doesn't even start, for example), `git bisect skip` picks a nearby one instead.

The real power is **`git bisect run <script>`**. A **script** here is a small program, often a few terminal commands, that checks for the bug.
