Git runs it at each step and reads its **exit code**: the number every program reports when it finishes. `0` means good, `125` means skip, and any other code from 1 to 127 means bad. An automated test that fails when the bug is present makes a perfect script, and the whole hunt runs unattended.

Bisect works best when every commit works and passes its tests on its own, one more reason for small, self-contained commits. In histories full of merges, `git bisect start --first-parent` follows only the main line, so it tells you which *merged branch* caused the problem.

The words don't have to be good and bad: `git bisect start --term-old=slow --term-new=fast` finds when something *improved*.
concepts.code:
cat > /tmp/check.sh <<'END'
#!/bin/sh
make -s build || exit 125          # can't build: skip this commit
./bin/app --selftest-date-parsing  # exits non-zero when the bug is present
END
chmod +x /tmp/check.sh

git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0       # bad, then good
git bisect run /tmp/check.sh
# 7e1f3c2 is the first bad commit
# Author: ... Date: ...  "Switch date parser to strptime"
git bisect log > bisect.txt        # keep a record
git bisect reset
takeaways: Bisect halves the suspect range each step: 1,000 commits take about 10 tests
git bisect run automates it: exit 0 good, 125 skip, 1-127 bad
Always finish with git bisect reset
pitfalls: Writing a run script that fails for unrelated reasons (like the program not building at all), so bisect blames the wrong commit — exit 125 to skip.

quiz.q: In git bisect run, what should the script exit with when a commit can't be tested?
quiz.explain: 125 tells bisect to skip the commit; 0 means good and other codes up to 127 mean bad.

quiz.q: About how many test steps does bisect need for 1,000 candidate commits?
quiz.explain: Each step halves the range, and halving 1,000 ten times gets you down to one.

concepts.name: Multiple working trees
concepts.summary: Check out several branches at once in separate folders that share one repository with git worktree.
concepts.why: Look at someone's branch or fix an urgent problem in the live version without stashing or disturbing the branch you're in the middle of.
concepts.body:
Normally a repository has one working tree, so switching branches means stashing or committing your current state, and anything running from your files, such as a long build or a live preview of your app, gets disrupted. **`git worktree`** lets one repository have several working trees, each with its own branch checked out, in different directories.

```bash
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login origin/main
```

That creates folder `../app-hotfix`, a new branch `hotfix/login` from `origin/main`, and checks it out there. Commits made in either folder go into the same repository, so they are immediately visible from the other; no pushing or fetching between them.

Management commands:

- `git worktree list`: all worktrees, their paths and branches.
- `git worktree remove ../app-hotfix`: delete the folder and Git's records of it (refuses if it has uncommitted changes, unless `--force`).
- `git worktree prune`: clean up Git's records of folders you deleted by hand.
- `git worktree add --detach ../tmp v2.3.0`: a throwaway checkout of a tag.

Rules and gotchas:

- A branch can be checked out in **only one** worktree at a time; Git refuses a second, to stop two folders from fighting over the same branch.
- Worktrees share the stored history, branches, settings and stashes, so they are far cheaper than a second clone.
- Each worktree has its own staging area and `HEAD`. Untracked or ignored files, such as downloaded add-ons in `node_modules`, belong to one folder, so you may need to download them again.

Worktrees are also a natural fit for running several tools, or several AI coding assistants, on different branches at the same time.
concepts.code:
# In ~/src/app, mid-feature with a live preview of the app running
git fetch origin
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login origin/main
cd ../app-hotfix
# ... fix, commit, push ...
git push -u origin hotfix/login
cd ../app
git worktree list
# /home/me/src/app         5d2e9f1 [feature/search]
# /home/me/src/app-hotfix  c81a7d3 [hotfix/login]
git worktree remove ../app-hotfix
takeaways: One repository, many checked-out folders, shared history and branches
A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time
Remove with git worktree remove, not by deleting the folder (or prune afterwards)
pitfalls: Expecting ignored files like node_modules or .env to exist in the new worktree — each folder has its own.

quiz.q: You try git worktree add ../x main while main is checked out in your current folder. What happens?
options: Both folders share main and stay in sync
Git refuses because main is already checked out
main is copied to a new branch main-2
The current folder switches to detached HEAD
quiz.explain: A branch can only be checked out in one worktree at a time.

concepts.name: Submodules
concepts.summary: Embed another repository at a pinned commit with git submodule, and keep it updated correctly.
concepts.why: Projects that include another project's code at an exact version often use submodules, and they confuse people who don't know how they work.
concepts.body:
A **submodule** is a Git repository nested inside another at a fixed path. The parent repository doesn't store the submodule's files; it stores a special entry (a "gitlink", file mode `160000`) recording **one exact commit** of the child, plus the URL in a `.gitmodules` file.

Adding one:

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/sdk.git vendor/sdk
git commit -m "Add sdk submodule"
```

Cloning a repository with submodules needs an extra step, or the folders stay empty:

- `git clone --recurse-submodules <url>`, or after a plain clone:
- `git submodule update --init --recursive`.

The key mental model: the parent **pins** a commit. Inside `vendor/sdk`, the submodule is usually in detached HEAD at that pinned commit. To upgrade:

```bash
cd vendor/sdk && git fetch && git switch --detach v1.5.0
cd ../.. && git add vendor/sdk && git commit -m "Bump sdk to v1.5.0"
```

`git submodule update --remote` does the fetch and checkout for you, following the branch configured in `.gitmodules`.

When teammates pull a commit that moved the pin, their submodule doesn't follow automatically; they run `git submodule update`, or set `submodule.recurse true` so pull, switch and friends do it.

Common traps: committing in the submodule but forgetting to push it (others then can't fetch the pinned commit), and forgetting to commit the new pin in the parent. `git status` and `git diff --submodule` show when a pin changed. If you don't need a separate repository pinned to an exact commit, letting a package manager (a tool that downloads the add-on code a project uses) fetch it is usually simpler.
concepts.code:
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:acme/firmware.git
cd firmware
git submodule status
#  4c1d2e3 vendor/sdk (v1.4.0)

git config --global submodule.recurse true   # pull/switch update submodules

git submodule update --remote vendor/sdk     # move to tip of tracked branch
git diff --submodule
# Submodule vendor/sdk 4c1d2e3..9a0b7f1: ...
git add vendor/sdk
git commit -m "Bump sdk"
takeaways: The parent stores a pinned commit (gitlink) plus the URL in .gitmodules
Clone with --recurse-submodules or run submodule update --init --recursive
Bumping = change the checkout inside, then commit the new pin in the parent
Push the submodule commit before pushing the parent
pitfalls: Committing a new pin to a submodule commit that was never pushed — everyone else's update fails.

quiz.q: What does the parent repository record about a submodule?
options: A full copy of the submodule's files
Only the URL; it always uses the latest commit
The URL and one exact commit ID
A zip of the submodule's history
quiz.explain: The gitlink entry pins a commit; .gitmodules holds the URL.

concepts.name: Git hooks
concepts.summary: Run small programs automatically at moments like pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push to check work before it's shared.
concepts.why: Hooks catch style problems, bad messages and failing tests before they leave your computer.
concepts.body:
**Git hooks** are small programs, usually short scripts, that Git runs automatically at certain moments. They live in `.git/hooks/` (which comes with `.sample` example files) or in a folder you choose with `core.hooksPath`. A hook is any file named after its moment and marked as runnable; its first line, such as `#!/bin/sh`, says which language it's written in.

Common hooks on your own computer:

- `pre-commit`: runs before Git asks for the commit message. If it fails (ends with an exit code other than 0), the commit is cancelled. Ideal for tools that check code style or tidy its layout.
- `prepare-commit-msg` / `commit-msg`: change or check the message, for example to require a ticket number. `commit-msg` is given the location of a file holding the message, as `$1`.
- `pre-push`: runs before anything is sent; run the quicker tests here.
- `post-checkout` / `post-merge`: run after switching branches or pulling, for example to download add-ons again when the list of them changed.

Servers have their own hooks (`pre-receive`, `update`, `post-receive`). Hosting sites offer them as settings instead: protected branches that refuse direct pushes, required checks, and messages sent to other services when something happens.

Two facts shape how hooks are used in teams:

- **Hooks are not cloned.** `.git/hooks` isn't part of the history, so to share them, commit a folder such as `.githooks/` and have everyone run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, or use a hook manager like pre-commit, Husky or Lefthook that installs them.
- **Hooks can be skipped.** `git commit --no-verify` (`-n`) skips `pre-commit` and `commit-msg`; `git push --no-verify` skips `pre-push`. So hooks are a convenience for fast feedback, and the checks the server runs on every push (CI) remain the real gate.

Keep hooks fast, a couple of seconds at most, and check only staged files, or people will start using `--no-verify` out of habit.
concepts.code:
mkdir -p .githooks
cat > .githooks/commit-msg <<'END'
#!/bin/sh
# Require "ABC-123: summary" style messages
if ! head -1 "$1" | grep -qE '^[A-Z]+-[0-9]+: .+'; then
  echo "commit-msg: start the message with a ticket ID, e.g. 'ABC-12: Fix login'" >&2
  exit 1
fi
END
chmod +x .githooks/commit-msg          # mark the file as runnable
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
git add .githooks && git commit -m "ABC-7: Add commit-msg hook"
git commit -m "oops"        # rejected by the hook
takeaways: A hook is a runnable file named after its moment, in .git/hooks or core.hooksPath
A failing pre-commit, commit-msg or pre-push hook cancels the action
Hooks aren't cloned; share them via core.hooksPath or a hook manager
--no-verify skips them, so server-side checks must still enforce rules
pitfalls: Forgetting chmod +x on the hook file — Git silently ignores hook files that aren't marked as runnable.

quiz.q: Why can't you rely on client-side hooks to enforce a policy?
options: Developers can skip them with --no-verify and they aren't cloned
Git deletes them after each commit
They run after the commit is pushed
quiz.explain: Hooks live only on each computer and can be skipped; checks on the server must enforce the rules.

quiz.q: Where does a commit-msg hook find the message it should check?
options: It is typed into the hook from the keyboard
In a file whose path is passed as the first argument
quiz.explain: Git writes the message to a file and passes that file's location as $1.

concepts.name: Branching strategies
concepts.summary: Compare trunk-based development, GitHub flow and Git flow, and choose one that fits how you release.
concepts.why: A shared branching convention decides how painful merges, releases and hotfixes are for the whole team.
concepts.body:
Git doesn't impose a workflow; teams agree on one. The main families:

**Trunk-based development**: everyone integrates into `main` (the trunk) at least daily, via very short-lived branches or directly. Unfinished features hide behind **feature flags**, on/off switches in the app's settings that keep new code turned off until it's ready, rather than living on long branches. It needs good automated tests and CI, and it keeps merges painless because nothing drifts apart for long. It is the norm for teams that release many times a day.

**GitHub flow**: `main` is always ready to **deploy** (release to users); every change is a branch plus a pull request; after review and passing checks it is merged and deployed. Essentially trunk-based with PRs. A good default for web services and most teams.

**Git flow**: long-lived `develop` and `main` branches, plus `feature/*`, `release/*` and `hotfix/*` branches with prescribed merges between them. It suits software that ships numbered versions on a schedule and must support several in parallel, but it adds ceremony and long-lived divergence. Its own author has said it is overkill for web apps that release continuously.

**Release branches** combine with any of these: cut `release/2.4` from `main` at release time, stabilise and patch it (copying individual fixes over from `main` with cherry-pick), and tag versions on it.

How to choose:

- Deploy continuously? Trunk-based or GitHub flow.
- Maintain several shipped versions at once (mobile apps, libraries, software customers install themselves)? Add release branches, or Git flow.
- Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived, protect `main` (required reviews and checks), and pick one PR merge style.

The strongest predictor of merge pain is branch lifetime, not the strategy's name.
takeaways: Trunk-based: integrate daily, hide unfinished work behind feature flags
GitHub flow: main always ready to release, branch + PR + deploy
Git flow and release branches suit versioned, multi-version products
Short-lived branches matter more than the strategy's name
pitfalls: Adopting Git flow for a continuously deployed web app and living with permanent develop/main drift.

quiz.q: A team deploys a web service many times a day. Which approach usually fits best?
options: Git flow with develop and release branches
Trunk-based or GitHub flow with feature flags
quiz.explain: Releasing many times a day favours short-lived branches merged into an always-releasable main.

quiz.q: What lets trunk-based teams merge unfinished features safely?
options: Feature flags that keep the code inactive
Keeping the feature on a branch for months
quiz.explain: The code ships switched off and is turned on when ready, so the branch never needs to live long.

concepts.name: The object model: blobs, trees, commits
concepts.summary: Git stores four kinds of Git objects, each under a hash of its content; commits point to trees, trees to blobs and subtrees.
concepts.why: Knowing how Git stores things explains why branches are cheap, why history rewriting changes IDs, and how recovery works.
concepts.body:
At its core Git is a store where every item is filed under an ID calculated from its own content: a hash, SHA-1 by default (with protection against deliberately forged collisions; repositories can opt into SHA-256 with `git init --object-format=sha256`). This is called **content-addressed** storage. Same content, same ID, stored once. Each stored item is a **Git object**.

There are four object types:

- **blob**: the raw contents of a file. No name, no permissions; two identical files anywhere in history are one blob.
- **tree**: one folder's listing. Each entry has a mode saying what it is (`100644` normal file, `100755` runnable program, `040000` subfolder, `120000` shortcut to another file, `160000` submodule), a name and an object ID.
- **commit**: points to one top-level tree (the snapshot), zero or more parent commits, author and committer with their dates and times, and the message.
- **tag** (annotated): points to an object, with tagger, message and optional signature.

An object's ID is the hash of a short header like `blob 12\0` followed by its content. Because a commit contains its tree's ID and its parents' IDs, its hash covers the entire snapshot and all of the history behind it. (A structure where each ID covers everything beneath it is called a Merkle tree.) Changing one byte anywhere changes the ID of every commit that comes after it. That's why rebases produce new commits, and why one commit ID identifies the full history behind it.

You can explore with **plumbing commands**, Git's low-level commands meant for scripts and the curious:

- `git cat-file -t <id>` gives the type; `-p` prints the content readably.
- `git ls-tree HEAD` lists the top-level tree.
- `git hash-object -w file` stores a blob and prints its ID.
- `git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}` gives a commit's tree ID.

Branches and tags are just names pointing into this web of objects; Git's general word for such names is **refs**. Everything else in Git is built on these few objects.
concepts.code:
git cat-file -p HEAD
# tree 8f3e1a...
# parent 3f9a2c1...
# author Ada <ada@example.com> 1760000000 +0200
# committer Ada <ada@example.com> 1760000000 +0200
#
# Add search index
git cat-file -p 'HEAD^{tree}'
# 100644 blob 5d1f0c...    README.md
# 040000 tree 2b7e94...    src
echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin   # ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha1sum        # same ID: header + content
git cat-file -t ce01362                   # blob
takeaways: Four object types: blob (content), tree (directory), commit, annotated tag
Object ID = hash of a type header + content, so identical content is stored once
Commits hash their tree and parents, so one ID pins all history
cat-file -p, ls-tree and hash-object let you inspect it directly
pitfalls: Thinking Git stores diffs between versions — objects are full snapshots; differences only appear later, as a space-saving trick inside packfiles.

quiz.q: Two different files in different directories have exactly the same content. How many blobs does Git store?
options: One per commit that contains them
quiz.explain: Blobs are addressed by content only; names live in trees.

quiz.q: Why does editing an old commit's message change the IDs of all later commits?
options: Messages are stored in every later commit
Each commit includes its parent's ID in the data that is hashed
quiz.explain: A new parent ID changes the child's content, hence its hash, cascading up the chain.

concepts.name: Refs, packfiles and garbage collection
concepts.summary: How Git stores refs (loose files, packed-refs, reftable) and Git objects (loose files, compressed packfiles), and what clean-up does.
concepts.why: Understanding storage explains repository size, slow operations and what Git's clean-up and maintenance commands actually do.
concepts.body:
**Refs** are names for object IDs. Traditionally each one is a small file: `.git/refs/heads/main` contains a commit ID, `.git/refs/tags/v1.0` a tag or commit ID, `.git/refs/remotes/origin/main` the remote-tracking branch. `.git/HEAD` is usually a **symbolic ref**, holding the name of another ref: `ref: refs/heads/main`.

With thousands of refs, Git moves them into one `.git/packed-refs` file; a separate ref file, if present, wins over its packed entry. Newer Git also offers **reftable** (`git init --ref-format=reftable`), a compact storage format that copes with millions of refs and updates several at once, all or nothing.

**Objects** start out **loose**: one compressed file each (compressed with zlib), at `.git/objects/ab/cdef...`, where the first two characters of the ID name the folder. That is simple but wasteful when there are many similar versions of a file.

**Packfiles** fix that. `git gc`, `git repack` and network transfers bundle objects into `.git/objects/pack/pack-*.pack`, with a matching `.idx` file that says where each object sits. Inside a pack, an object can be stored as a **delta**: just its differences from a similar Git object, often an older or newer version of the same file. Clones and fetches send packs, which is why they are compact.

**Clean-up** (`git gc`, which Git also starts by itself now and then, controlled by `gc.auto`) packs loose objects, packs refs, trims old reflog entries and deletes unreachable objects older than a grace period (two weeks by default). `git maintenance` schedules smaller versions of these jobs to run in the background.

Diagnostics:

- `git count-objects -vH`: size of loose vs packed objects.
- `git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/*.idx | sort -k3 -n | tail`: the largest objects.
- `git for-each-ref`: list refs, whatever format stores them.
concepts.code:
cat .git/HEAD                     # ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main          # 9c1e2ab4f... (if not packed)
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname) %(objectname:short)' refs/heads
git count-objects -vH
# count: 312  size: 1.4 MiB  in-pack: 48210  size-pack: 61.0 MiB
git gc                            # pack objects + refs, delete unreachable ones
git count-objects -vH             # count: 0 ...
# Biggest objects in the pack
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx | sort -k3 -n | tail -3
takeaways: Refs map names to IDs: loose files, packed-refs, or reftable
HEAD is normally a symbolic ref to the current branch
Packfiles hold delta-compressed objects; loose objects are one compressed file each
Clean-up packs objects, trims old reflog entries and deletes unreachable objects
pitfalls: Editing ref files by hand — use git update-ref so packed-refs, reftable and the reflog stay consistent.

quiz.q: Where are deltas between file versions stored?
options: Inside packfiles, as a storage optimization
quiz.explain: Objects are full snapshots; packfiles store some as differences to save space and transfer time.

quiz.q: What does a symbolic ref like HEAD usually contain?
options: The name of another ref, such as refs/heads/main
quiz.explain: HEAD normally points at a branch name, which in turn points at a commit.

concepts.name: How merges really work
concepts.summary: The ort strategy, merge bases and criss-cross merges, strategy vs strategy options, rerere and merge-tree.
concepts.why: When merges behave surprisingly, these internals explain why and give you the tools to control them.
concepts.body:
A merge combines three trees: the **merge base** and the two tips. `git merge-base A B` shows the base; for each path Git takes whichever side changed it, and where both changed it, merges line by line. Conflicts are blocks of lines that both sides changed differently.

Git's default strategy is **ort** ("Ostensibly Recursive's Twin"), the default since Git 2.34 and much faster than the older `recursive`, which recent versions treat as a synonym for ort. Its main jobs beyond the basic three-way merge:

- **Rename detection**: matching a deleted path to an added one with similar content, so an edit on one side follows a rename on the other.
- **Criss-cross merges**: when two branches have merged each other, there can be several "best" common ancestors. Ort merges those bases into a virtual base first, then merges against it.

Other strategies (`-s`): `octopus` merges several branches at once if there are no conflicts; `ours` records a merge but keeps your tree entirely, discarding the other side; `subtree` handles a project embedded in a subdirectory.

Don't confuse the **`-s ours` strategy** with the **`-X ours` option**. `-X ours` runs a normal ort merge but resolves *conflicting hunks only* in your favour; non-conflicting changes from the other side still come in. `-X theirs` is the mirror, and `-X ignore-space-change` and `-X patience` are other options.

**rerere** ("reuse recorded resolution", `rerere.enabled true`) remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it the next time the same conflict appears, which is very useful when repeatedly rebasing a long branch.

`git merge-tree --write-tree A B` performs a merge without touching the working tree or staging area and prints the result tree and any conflicts. Hosting sites use it to tell whether a pull request can be merged.
concepts.code:
git merge-base main feature                 # 3f9a2c1...
git merge-base --all main feature           # several = criss-cross history

git merge -X ours feature       # conflicts resolved to our side, rest merged
git merge -s ours legacy        # record merge, keep our tree completely

git config --global rerere.enabled true

# Test-merge without touching your files (exit code 1 = conflicts)
git merge-tree --write-tree main feature
# 4b0e3c...                     <- resulting tree ID
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in billing.py
takeaways: ort is the default strategy; it detects renames and handles multiple bases
-s ours discards the other side entirely; -X ours only settles conflicts
rerere replays conflict resolutions you made before
merge-tree --write-tree merges without touching your files
pitfalls: Using -s ours when you meant -X ours and silently dropping all of the other branch's changes.

quiz.q: What does git merge -X theirs feature do to non-conflicting changes made on your current branch?
options: Keeps them; only conflicting hunks take feature's version
quiz.explain: -X theirs only affects how conflicting hunks are resolved; everything else merges normally.

quiz.q: When does a merge have more than one merge base?
options: When either branch has merge commits
In criss-cross histories where branches merged each other
quiz.explain: Criss-cross merges leave several equally good common ancestors, which ort merges into a virtual base.

concepts.name: Rewriting history at scale
concepts.summary: Remove secrets or huge files from all of history with git filter-repo, and coordinate the force-push safely.
concepts.why: Leaked credentials and bloated repos need whole-history rewrites, which are easy to get wrong.
concepts.body:
Interactive rebase edits a handful of commits. To change **every** commit, for example to remove a leaked password or access key, purge a 2 GB video, or extract a subdirectory into its own repository, you need a filtering tool.

`git filter-branch` exists but is slow and full of pitfalls; its own documentation recommends **git filter-repo**, installed separately (it is written in Python: `pip install git-filter-repo`), fast and safe by default. Common operations:

- `--path secrets.env --invert-paths`: delete a path from all history.
- `--strip-blobs-bigger-than 50M`: drop huge files.
- `--replace-text expressions.txt`: replace pieces of text, such as access keys, in every version of every file.
- `--path src/lib/ --path-rename src/lib/:`: keep one directory and make it the root.
- `--mailmap`: fix author names and emails.

Every rewritten commit gets a new ID, so this is a coordinated migration, not a quick fix:

- Work in a fresh clone (filter-repo insists on it, and removes the `origin` remote so you can't push by accident).
- **Change the leaked secrets first.** Other copies may still hold the old commits: teammates' clones, forks, saved copies on automated build machines, and the hosting site's records of pull requests. Rewriting doesn't un-leak anything.
- Announce a freeze, force-push all branches and tags (`git push --force --all` and `--tags`), and have everyone re-clone. An old clone merged back in reintroduces the purged history.
- Ask the hosting site's support to delete its stored copies where needed.

Alternatives: `git replace` grafts history without rewriting (for example to stitch an archived history onto a fresh start), and for big files such as videos from now on, **Git LFS** (Large File Storage) keeps them outside the repository's own storage.
concepts.code:
pip install git-filter-repo
git clone --mirror git@github.com:acme/app.git app-clean
cd app-clean

# One pass: drop a file, huge blobs, and redact key-like strings
printf 'regex:AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}==>REDACTED\n' > ../expr.txt
git filter-repo --path config/prod.env --invert-paths \
  --strip-blobs-bigger-than 50M --replace-text ../expr.txt
git log --all --oneline -S AKIA        # verify: no output

git remote add origin git@github.com:acme/app.git
git push --force --mirror origin      # after secrets are rotated and team is warned
takeaways: Use git filter-repo, not filter-branch, for whole-history rewrites
Change leaked secrets: rewriting history doesn't un-leak them
Every commit ID changes: freeze, force-push everything, everyone re-clones
pitfalls: Letting a teammate push from an old clone after the rewrite, which brings the purged commits back.

quiz.q: You purged a leaked API key from history and force-pushed. What else is mandatory?
options: Running git gc on your laptop
Revoking/rotating the key, since copies may exist elsewhere
quiz.explain: Forks, clones and saved copies may still contain the old commits, so the key must be treated as stolen.

concepts.name: Performance on big repositories
concepts.summary: Make huge repos fast with partial and shallow clones, sparse checkout, commit-graph, fsmonitor and git maintenance.
concepts.why: Huge repositories, such as one repository holding a whole company's code, become unusable without these features.
concepts.body:
Big repositories are slow for different reasons, and each has a remedy.

**Too much history or too many blobs to download:**

- **Partial clone** `git clone --filter=blob:none <url>` downloads all commits and trees but fetches file contents lazily, on demand. History commands still work. This is usually the best choice for developers.
- `--filter=tree:0` goes further (folder listings are fetched on demand too); suited to automated build machines that check out one commit and throw it away.
- **Shallow clone** `--depth=1` truncates history entirely. Fast for automated builds, but `log`, `blame` and merges with old branches suffer; `git fetch --unshallow` repairs it.

**Too many files in the working tree:**

- **Sparse checkout** `git sparse-checkout set --cone services/api libs/common` checks out only the directories you need; with cone mode and a sparse index, commands that read the staging area only do work for what you checked out.

**Slow status, log and graph commands:**

- `core.fsmonitor true` starts Git's built-in file watcher (macOS, Windows), a background program that notices changes as they happen, so `git status` doesn't have to check every file. `core.untrackedCache true` remembers earlier searches for untracked files.
- The **commit-graph** file speeds up `log`, finding merge bases, and checking which commits lead to which; `fetch.writeCommitGraph true` keeps it current.

**Keeping it all tuned:** `git maintenance start` registers the repository for background tasks (prefetch, commit-graph, loose-object packing, incremental repack) through your computer's built-in task scheduler, so you never wait for a big clean-up.

**`scalar`** (shipped with Git) bundles these: `scalar clone <url>` sets up partial clone, sparse checkout, fsmonitor and maintenance in one command.

Large files such as images and videos are a separate problem: use Git LFS so they live outside the repository's own storage.
concepts.code:
# Developer clone of a big monorepo
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse git@github.com:acme/mono.git
cd mono
git sparse-checkout set --cone services/api libs/common
git config core.fsmonitor true
git config core.untrackedCache true
git maintenance start          # background prefetch, commit-graph, repack

# CI: fastest possible checkout of one commit
git clone --depth=1 --filter=blob:none https://github.com/acme/mono.git

# Or all of the above in one go
scalar clone https://github.com/acme/mono.git
takeaways: Partial clone (--filter=blob:none) fetches file contents on demand
Shallow clones are for automated builds; they cripple history commands
Sparse checkout + sparse index shrink the working tree and staging area
fsmonitor, commit-graph and git maintenance keep daily commands fast
pitfalls: Using --depth=1 clones for daily development and then fighting broken merges and missing history.

quiz.q: Which clone keeps full commit history but downloads file contents only when needed?
quiz.explain: A blobless partial clone has every commit and tree; blobs are fetched lazily.

quiz.q: What does git maintenance start do?
options: Schedules background tasks such as prefetch and commit-graph updates
quiz.explain: It registers the repository with the system scheduler for incremental maintenance.
